"Broadband correlation between every pair of separated stems. Independent parts sit near 0 (normal). A strongly NEGATIVE pair (<= -0.65) is inverted: the two partly cancel when summed, the classic flipped-polarity or misaligned-mic problem. A strongly POSITIVE pair (>= +0.65) shares content - bleed or a doubled part.\n\nNeeds AI-separated (Demucs) stems; the approximate harmonic/percussive split is not a source separation, so it is not checked." = "Broadband correlation between every pair of separated stems. Independent parts sit near 0 (normal). A strongly NEGATIVE pair (<= -0.65) is inverted: the two partly cancel when summed, the classic flipped-polarity or misaligned-mic problem. A strongly POSITIVE pair (>= +0.65) shares content - bleed or a doubled part.\n\nNeeds AI-separated (Demucs) stems; the approximate harmonic/percussive split is not a source separation, so it is not checked."

"Calibrated monitoring is the root of consistent decisions: when a known signal level always produces the same SPL in the room, your ears judge every mix against the same reference instead of today's volume-knob mood.\n\nThe K-System-style routine: 1) play the -20 dBFS RMS pink noise through your normal playback path at your normal monitor gain, one speaker at a time if you can; 2) read SPL at the mix position (any phone SPL app: C-weighted, slow); 3) enter the reading. The wizard tells you how far you are from the reference for your room size, and saves the profile so the fatigue coach and future sessions know your real monitoring level.\n\nReferences: large control room 83 dB SPL per speaker; mid room 79 dB; small/home room 76 dB." = "Calibrated monitoring is the root of consistent decisions: when a known signal level always produces the same SPL in the room, your ears judge every mix against the same reference instead of today's volume-knob mood.\n\nThe K-System-style routine: 1) play the -20 dBFS RMS pink noise through your normal playback path at your normal monitor gain, one speaker at a time if you can; 2) read SPL at the mix position (any phone SPL app: C-weighted, slow); 3) enter the reading. The wizard tells you how far you are from the reference for your room size, and saves the profile so the fatigue coach and future sessions know your real monitoring level.\n\nReferences: large control room 83 dB SPL per speaker; mid room 79 dB; small/home room 76 dB."

"Continuous short-term (3 s window, 1 s hop) K-weighted LUFS reading across the whole track (teal) -- a mastering-meter-style history graph, finer-grained than the Loudness Arc panel's per-section buckets. The dashed line marks the track's integrated LUFS. The grey line is the rolling peak/RMS crest factor over the same windows, own 0-24 dB scale -- where dynamics actually get squashed, not just the whole-track average. The three thin heatmap lanes at the bottom show per-window loudness (teal), squashing (grey), and harshness (red), so localized issues stay visible even when the curves overlap. The right strip is a probability-density histogram of the LUFS values; red ticks along the top mark inter-sample true-peak overshoots past -1 dBTP." = "Continuous short-term (3 s window, 1 s hop) K-weighted LUFS reading across the whole track (teal) -- a mastering-meter-style history graph, finer-grained than the Loudness Arc panel's per-section buckets. The dashed line marks the track's integrated LUFS. The grey line is the rolling peak/RMS crest factor over the same windows, own 0-24 dB scale -- where dynamics actually get squashed, not just the whole-track average. The three thin heatmap lanes at the bottom show per-window loudness (teal), squashing (grey), and harshness (red), so localized issues stay visible even when the curves overlap. Most arrangement problems are element problems: four strong elements at once reads as crowded; rhythm with no foundation has no anchor; long stretches with no lead lose the listener. Flags below name the exact moments." = "Every arrangement is built from five elements: the FOUNDATION (bass + kick), the RHYTHM (drums/percussion), the PAD (sustained chords/beds), the LEAD (the element carrying the ear - here, the vocal stem), and FILLS (transient ear candy between lead phrases).\n\nThis grid shows each element's energy share across the song from the separated stems. "Front-to-back staging, measured from the three cues that create depth perception: reverberant tail (wetness), high-frequency rolloff (darkness), and transient bluntness (softness). Front elements are dry, bright, and sharp; back elements are wet, dark, and smeared.\n\nA great mix uses the whole ladder - lead vocal near the front, pads and rooms behind. If every stem sits on the same rung, the mix reads as flat no matter how good the balance is. Requires separated stems." = "Front-to-back staging, measured from the three cues that create depth perception: reverberant tail (wetness), high-frequency rolloff (darkness), and transient bluntness (softness). If every stem sits on the same rung, the mix reads as flat no matter how good the balance is. Requires separated stems."

It is measured only where the audio decays freely - stops, endings and isolated hits - and the median of those decays is shown (dense material with no gaps has no measurable RT60, and says so).\n\nThe tail ratio is the energy between hits relative to the hits themselves: a high ratio means a wet, washy mix where the space may mask detail; a low one means dry and upfront. Use it with the Depth Ladder to judge front-to-back staging." = "RT60 is how long the sound takes to decay by 60 dB. "Scans the source file for AI-generation evidence in three classes. Provenance: container metadata naming a generator, a decoded watermark, a validated model - only this can read 'likely AI-generated'. Heuristic artifacts: codec-reconstruction residue and similar AI-typical signatures - at most 'AI-typical artifacts found'. Production-style observations (lossy low-pass, constant noise floor, flat dynamics, looped sections) are shown as context with no weight - human records do all of these.\n\nThe number is an uncalibrated heuristic signal score, not a probability. A checklist row reads 'resembles X' unless provenance names the service. Detectors that did not run are listed. Clipping events are counted with their timestamps." = "Scans the source file for AI-generation evidence in three classes. Provenance: container metadata naming a generator, a decoded watermark, a validated model - only this can read 'likely AI-generated'. Heuristic artifacts: codec-reconstruction residue and similar AI-typical signatures - at most 'AI-typical artifacts found'. Production-style observations (lossy low-pass, constant noise floor, flat dynamics, looped sections) are shown as context with no weight - human records do all of these.\n\nThe number is an uncalibrated heuristic signal score, not a probability. A checklist row reads 'resembles X' unless provenance names the service. Detectors that did not run are listed. Clipping events are counted with their timestamps."

"The phase relationship between the kick and the bass fundamental in the sub/low band (< 120 Hz). When they're in phase the low end sums and hits hard; out of phase, it partially cancels on mono, club, and phone systems - the classic \"the bass disappears on the big rig\" problem.\n\nThe goniometer plots kick (x) against bass (y): a cloud along the rising diagonal is in phase, along the falling diagonal is out of phase, a round blob is uncorrelated. The strip below tracks their correlation over time. Kick is approximated by low-passing the drums stem; requires separated stems." = "The phase relationship between the kick and the bass fundamental in the sub/low band (< 120 Hz).
